title: Injury Severity Score (ISS)
sources: Baker SP et al. J Trauma 1974; AAAM Abbreviated Injury Scale
purpose: An anatomic trauma severity score: take the highest Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS, 1–6) grade in each of the three most severely injured body regions, square each, and sum. Range 3–75. Primarily a registry / benchmarking and research tool (feeds TRISS) — it is calculated after injuries are catalogued, not a bedside triage instrument.

inputs.label: Highest AIS in the worst-injured region (1 minor · 2 moderate · 3 serious · 4 severe · 5 critical · 6 unsurvivable)
Highest AIS in the second worst-injured region
Highest AIS in the third worst-injured region

interpretation.label: Minor trauma (ISS 1–8) — low mortality; injuries typically managed without critical care
Moderate trauma (ISS 9–15) — admission usual; mortality still low but rising
Major / severe trauma (ISS ≥ 16) — the conventional 'major trauma' threshold; substantial mortality and complication risk. Trauma-centre care, trauma team, ICU consideration
Profound / critical trauma (ISS ≥ 25) — high mortality; damage-control resuscitation and surgery, ICU

notes: The six AIS body regions: head/neck, face, chest, abdomen/pelvic contents, extremities/pelvic girdle, external/skin. If ANY region scores AIS 6, ISS is automatically set to 75. Only ONE injury per region counts (the highest) — ISS therefore under-represents multiple injuries within the same region; the New ISS (NISS = sum of squares of the three worst injuries regardless of region) corrects this and predicts mortality better. Use T-RTS / mechanism / physiology for actual field and ED triage.
buildNote: Formula engine — sum of squares of three AIS grades. Any AIS 6 → ISS 75 (note only; not auto-applied by the expression).
